Hast.et: 16th century, from Middle Low German hāst, from Middle Dutch haest, a borrowing from Old French haste, itself borrowed from Frankish *hai(f)st, from Proto-Germanic *haifstiz. See English haste for more.

Hase.et: From Middle High German has(e), from Old High German haso, from Proto-West Germanic *hasō, from Proto-Germanic *hesô, from an Indo-European root originally meaning grey.
German and Jewish surname, from the noun meaning "hare" (see Etymology 1 above). Occasionally calqued from Lower Sorbian Zajac, of the same meaning.
From the same root as the animal name, meaning “grey”, an adjective Proto-West Germanic *hasu (“grey”).

Hasenscharte.et: From Middle High German hasinscharte. By surface analysis, Hase (“hare”) + -n- + Scharte (“notch”). So called because of the similarity to the outer form of a hare’s lip. Compare already Old English hærsceard.

s: Wann i heute spazieren geh und an, an Flamo hob im Magen, an Hunger, dann sag i einfach: ‘Jetzt gemma auf a Haße’, net, und dann gehst einfach auf a Haße, net.
Hasse.et: From the Viennese dialect word hass (“hot”); thus literally, “a hot one”.

s: Es gibt nichts, das ich mehr hasse als Wespen.
There is nothing I hate more than wasps.
Die Rabenkrähen hassten auf den Waldkauz.
The carrion crows mobbed the tawny owl.

Hass.et: From Middle High German haȥ, from Old High German haȥ. Compare Dutch haat, English hate, Danish had; also Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐍄𐌹𐍃 (hatis), Old Norse hatr, Old English hete, Old Saxon heti.

Haselnuss.et: From Middle High German haselnuz, from Old High German hasalnuz. Analysable as Hasel + Nuss. Cognate with Dutch hazelnoot, English hazelnut.

Hasel.et: From Middle High German hasel, from Old High German hasal, from Proto-West Germanic *hasl.
Inherited from Middle High German hasel, from Old High German hasala f.

hässlich.et: From Middle High German hezzelich, hazzelich, hazlich, hezlich, from Old High German hazlīh. Equivalent to Hass + -lich.

hastig.et: From Middle High German hastic, hastec. Analysable as Hast + -ig. Compare Middle Low German hastich (whence German Low German hastig, haastig).

Churchgoers had to cross the cemetery surrounding the church and thereby overheard the hateful tirade, in which the apostate priest mocked the teachings of the Church, especially confession, as superstition.
Die Informatikerin hat bis Mai bei Facebook gearbeitet, lange in einer Abteilung zur Eindämmung von Hassrede und Lügen.
The computer scientist had been working for Facebook until May, for a long time she had been part of a department working to curb hate speech and lies.
Hassrede.et: Hass + Rede. The uncountable use is a semantic loan from English hate speech, though there exists an intermediate usage based on the indefinite plural.

s: Used at the end of a list: To emphasize its length; you name it.
In dem Laden verkaufen sie Obst, Gemüse, Brot und Brötchen, und haste nicht gesehen.
That store sells fruit, vegetables, bread and rolls, you name it!
Used at the end of a list: To indicate that some items were not named; whatnot, all that jazz, what have you.
Und zum Essen sind wir in ein schickes Restaurant mit Tischtüchern und Kerzen und haste nicht gesehen...
And then we went to eat in a fancy restaurant with tableclothes and candlelight and what have you...
haste nicht gesehen.et: Literally, “you didn't see (i.e. catch) [that]”, in reference to something happening so quickly that an onlooker fails to catch it.

s: Used to emphasize the speed or suddenness of an action; blammo just like that
